{{DISPLAYTITLE:θ<sub>10</sub>}}
In [[representation theory]], a branch of mathematics, '''θ<sub>10</sub>''' is a particular [[unitary representation]] of the [[symplectic group]] Sp<sub>4</sub>, which has some exceptional properties. The symplectic group Sp<sub>4</sub> is the set of 4&times;4 matrices that preserve a skew-symmetric non-degenerate matrix, but its unitary representations – that is, the ways of realizing that set as a group of [[linear operator]]s preserving the [[inner product]] in a [[Hilbert space]] – are often subtle. 

The notation θ<sub>10</sub> was first used for a complex irreducible representation of the finite group Sp<sub>4</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>), where '''F'''<sub>''q''</sub> is a [[finite field]] with ''q'' elements. In this finite-field case, for ''q'' odd, θ<sub>10</sub> has dimension ''q''(''q'' – 1)<sup>2</sup>/2. It is notable because it is simultaneously [[cuspidal representation|cuspidal]], [[unipotent representation|unipotent]], and degenerate, meaning that it has no [[Whittaker model]]. Related representations, also denoted θ<sub>10</sub>, occur for Sp<sub>4</sub> over [[local field|local]] and [[global field]]s.

==Finite-field case==

{{harvtxt|Srinivasan|1968}} introduced θ<sub>10</sub> in her determination of the irreducible characters of the finite symplectic group Sp<sub>4</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>) for ''q'' odd. She showed that θ<sub>10</sub> has degree
''q''(''q'' – 1)<sup>2</sup>/2.

The subscript 10 is historical. Srinivasan labelled certain characters of Sp<sub>4</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>) as θ<sub>1</sub>, θ<sub>2</sub>, ..., θ<sub>13</sub>; the tenth character in this list is the cuspidal unipotent character now known as θ<sub>10</sub>.

In the finite-field setting, θ<sub>10</sub> is the only cuspidal unipotent representation of Sp<sub>4</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>). It is also the smallest example of a cuspidal unipotent representation of a [[reductive group]] and the smallest example of a degenerate cuspidal representation. [[General linear group]]s do not have cuspidal unipotent representations, and they do not have degenerate cuspidal representations. Thus θ<sub>10</sub> exhibits features of the representation theory of general reductive groups that are absent for general linear groups.

==Construction==

One construction of θ<sub>10</sub> uses the [[Weil representation]] and [[Howe duality]]. Let ''V'' be a four-dimensional [[symplectic vector space]] over '''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>, and let ''E'' be a two-dimensional anisotropic [[quadratic space]] over '''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>. Then ''V'' ⊗ ''E'' is an eight-dimensional symplectic vector space.

The Weil representation of Sp(''V'' ⊗ ''E'') restricts to an action of Sp(''V'') × O(''E''). Since O(''E'') contains the special orthogonal group SO(''E'') as a subgroup of index two, the representation can be decomposed using the characters of SO(''E'') and the involution coming from the nontrivial coset of O(''E''). In this decomposition, one of the resulting irreducible Sp(''V'')-representations, usually denoted ''W''<sup>−</sup><sub>1</sub>, has dimension ''q''(''q'' – 1)<sup>2</sup>/2. Its character is the representation θ<sub>10</sub>.{{sfn|Deshpande|2008}}

==Properties==

The representation θ<sub>10</sub> is [[irreducible representation|irreducible]], so it has no nonzero proper invariant subspaces. It is [[cuspidal representation|cuspidal]], meaning that it does not arise from a proper [[Borel subgroup|parabolic subgroup]] by [[parabolic induction]]. Equivalently, in the finite-field setting, its restriction to the [[unipotent radical]] of a proper parabolic subgroup does not contain the trivial representation.

It is also degenerate: it does not admit a [[Whittaker model]]. For representations of [[reductive group]]s, the existence of a Whittaker model is often called genericity. Thus θ<sub>10</sub> is an example of a cuspidal but non-generic representation.

Finally, θ<sub>10</sub> is unipotent in the sense of [[Deligne–Lusztig theory]]: it occurs in the part of the character theory attached to the trivial character of a [[maximal torus]]. The simultaneous occurrence of all three properties – cuspidal, unipotent, and degenerate – is what makes θ<sub>10</sub> exceptional.

==Local and global analogues==

Representations also denoted θ<sub>10</sub> occur for Sp<sub>4</sub> over local and global fields. {{harvtxt|Howe|Piatetski-Shapiro|1979}} used such representations in their construction of counterexamples to the [[generalized Ramanujan conjecture]] for quasi-split groups. These examples showed that a naive generalization of the Ramanujan conjecture to all cuspidal automorphic representations of reductive groups could not hold without additional hypotheses, such as genericity.

{{harvtxt|Adams|2004}} described the real local representation θ<sub>10</sub> for the Lie group Sp<sub>4</sub>('''R'''). {{harvtxt|Kim|Piatetski-Shapiro|2001}} studied quadratic base change for θ<sub>10</sub>.
